The big thing is just learning to shoot the gun or bow. Guns are a little more accessible, and require less practice to get accurate with (especially with a good scope). But you have a couple of options. Probably the easiest thing would be to access someone you know (family member, friend of family, or neighbor) who has experience and ask them to show you the basics of using a rifle. They are stunningly simple. But most people know or have an older guy around who is typically happy to show what they know. Another option would be to use the internet. I don't know for certain, but would imagine there are plenty of guides out there on how to get into hunting, including using the rifle or bow. Lastly, you could actually enroll in a hunter's safety program. They're going to go through just about everything in that and you'll get a chance to shoot several different firearms (at least, they did that in my day).

But other than using the gun, its really only about a couple of things:

  • Location: you need a spot to hunt (friend or relative's property, your own, or state land)

  • Hunting Spot: build a simple blind, or purchase a tree stand; scour whatever the property is and look for signs of activity: tracks, droppings, rubs on trees. Use these to try to get an intuition for the trails deer walk. They do tend to be creatures of habit. Position your hunting spot with respect to that path. Camouflage the blind. Depending on what your state laws are, you could also bait leading up to start of the season and set up a trail camera (wonderful tools). See what kind of activity you're getting and what times of the day, and use this to further hone your spot selection.

  • Outerwear: get some basic camo gear. If you are using a blind, its not as essential.

That's just about it. Obviously, hunting can be an art, and you'll get more refined in your techniques, knowledge, and equipment as you go. But just getting out there and getting started is not rocket science at all. You've just got to make the decision to do it. Its about patience more than anything. You'll have days you'll go sit for 4 hours and see nothing but leaves drop. But for me, half of the enjoyment is just unplugging, getting away from people and just sitting in the woods/nature.

If you do decide to start hunting, make sure that you get familiar with your local laws. You'll be surprised at how many rules there are even for using your own private property. Its kind of ridiculous actually. For example, in MI you need to buy a license and tags for any deer you might kill. They used to have what was called a 'small game license' which has been transitioned to a 'base license'. Basically, people weren't buying small game licenses, so they just made them a 'base' license that you have to buy in addition to the others. Its fucking ridiculous.

There are two major components to avoiding the "gamey" taste. First is to pick the right animal for harvesting. If you want the best tasting meat, you pick a nice fat doe. Ethically, this can be difficult because removing a breeding doe reduces local populations more than a small buck. Because of that, I prefer the latter unless the area is heavily overpopulated.

Second is the field dress and prep; the key here is immediacy. Step one is to remove the scent glands on the inside of the legs, step two is draining the blood, and step three is removing the entrails. These all need to be done ASAP after death, and in the order listed.

My family always took the time to hang our animals for a few days to "cure". I was always told it was to help with the texture of the meat, not necessarily the flavor. But I've never had anyone complain that meat my family prepared was gamey, so take that as you will.

If you get meat that smells gamey, just rinse it with some vinegar before cooking. I'll usually just pour a little into bowl, dip the steaks in, give them a good rubbing with my bare hands, and then rinse the vinegar off with water. That'll kill a lot of that nasty taste/smell people associate with venison.
